Russian garrisons left in early 1918; British posts (Anzali) until May 1920.

controller_note: Persian Socialist Soviet Republic (Kuchek Khan, Ehsanollah Khan, Haydar Khan Amu-oghlu) under Red Army protection
note: The Red Army landed at Anzali on 18 May 1920; the Soviet Republic of Gilan was proclaimed at Rasht on 4-6 June. After the Feb 1921 Persian-Soviet treaty the Red Army left on 8 Sept 1921 and Reza Khan's forces took Rasht in October; Kuchek died in December 1921.

controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov column)
note: Baratov took Hamadan in December 1915 (sources: 3 or 15 Dec). The Russians evacuated it on 9 Aug 1916 (last troops marched out that afternoon) and the Ottoman XIII Corps entered on 10 Aug 1916 (Segal 2023, citing A.C. Edwards, an eyewitness).

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916

controller_note: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan)
note: Ottoman XIII Corps entered Hamadan on 10 Aug 1916 while Baratov's Russians held the Sultan Bulagh pass about 75 miles from Qazvin. The Ottoman advance halted at the end of its supply line; the sources consulted (Wikipedia 'Persian campaign (World War I)', citing Caven) have Baratov moving on Hamadan again in December 1916, and Hamadan changed hands that month. The end month is the least certain part (some accounts keep the Ottomans there into early 1917).

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
Ottoman entry 10 Aug 1916; Russian line at Sultan Bulagh

controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov corps, disintegrating)
note: Russian garrisons (Baratov's Caucasian Cavalry Corps) re-entered Hamadan in December 1916 and held it until the army dissolved in winter 1917-18. Start moved from 1917-03 to 1916-12 (see the Ottoman record above); low confidence.

controller_note: British (Dunsterforce, then Norperforce lines)
note: Dunsterville's advance party reached Hamadan in Feb 1918; the British kept Hamadan as a base on the Kermanshah-Qazvin line until Norperforce left on 21 April 1921.

controller_note: Britain (Royal Navy/Government of India coaling depot and naval base)
note: A telegraph station had been tolerated since the late 1860s; the coaling depot moved from Basidu to Henjam in 1911/12 and by 1913 it was the main British naval base. Persia had granted only a telegraph concession; Reza Shah demanded evacuation and the British abandoned the station in 1935.

controller_note: Iran (defenders) vs. Iraq (besiegers)
note: Iraqi forces encircled Abadan from late 1980 but never took the city; the siege was lifted on 27 Sept 1981 (Operation Samen-ol-A'emeh). Start date is the invasion date; full encirclement came later.

controller_note: Iraq
note: Iraq entered Dehloran, Qasr-e Shirin, Sumar, Naft Shahr, Sar-e Pol-e Zahab and Mousiyan on 12 July 1988 and withdrew from the towns after Iran accepted the ceasefire; but reports in August 1990 say Iraq still held about 2,600 km2 (1,000 sq mi) of Iranian territory, which it began to evacuate on 16-17 Aug 1990 (a UN report of 24 Sept 1990 said withdrawal was almost complete). Locations of the pockets were not identified in sources found. UNIIMOG's own background says that by end-September 1990 withdrawal to the international boundaries was 'almost complete' with a few locations where forces of each side were still on the wrong side, and that by end-January 1991 Iraq had withdrawn from 23 of 29 disputed positions (Iran from 13 of 17). The pockets were therefore a handful of border positions, not a large contiguous area, and the Aug 1990 '2,600 km2' figure comes from press reports of Saddam Hussein's offer. Record kept at low confidence.

cites.note: cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988

controller_note: Iraq
note: The Iraqi attack on Khorramshahr began on 22 Sept 1980; the city fell on 24 Oct (Iraqi control effectively complete 10 Nov) after a 34-day battle and was liberated on 24 May 1982 in Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas. Iraq announced its withdrawal from remaining Iranian territory on 20 June 1982.

controller_note: Iraq vs. Iran (Mehran changed hands several times)
note: Iraq captured Mehran in the 1980 invasion; Wikipedia ('Battle of Mehran (1986)') calls the May 1986 capture the third time Iraq took it, so Iraqi control before 1986 was not continuous, and the Mehran article says the Iraqis had been driven out by 1982-83. Dates of the first recapture are not established, so the whole span is shown as contested (low confidence).

controller_note: Iraq (II Corps)
note: Iraq recaptured Mehran on 15-19 May 1986 ("for the third time"); Iran retook the area in Operation Karbala-1 (30 June-3 July 1986) and defeated a Republican Guard counter-attack on 4 July.

controller_note: Iraqi forces with the Mojahedin-e Khalq (Operation Forty Stars)
note: On 18 June 1988 Iraq and the MEK crushed two Iranian divisions and seized Mehran; Iraqi regulars left after three days and the MEK stayed. Wikipedia says Iran retook Mehran in Operation Mersad (26 July); the end date is uncertain.

controller_note: Iraq
note: Iraqi forces held Bostan and parts of the Dasht-e Azadegan plain (the Susangerd salient). Iran relieved a siege of Susangerd in Nov 1980 and recaptured Bostan and 70 villages on 29 Nov-7 Dec 1981 (Operation Tariq al-Quds); the rest was cleared by June 1982. Holdings varied by month. Iranica ('Iraq vii'): after Fath ol-Mobin (22 March 1982, Shush-Dezful) and the 22 March offensive north of Bostan, the stage of 24 April-12 May 1982 'drove the Iraqi troops back to Khorramshahr from the Ahvaz-Susangird area'; the end is therefore May 1982 rather than Iraq's general withdrawal announcement in June. Khorramshahr itself (separate record) fell on 24-25 May.

controller_note: Iraq
note: Iraq took Qasr-e Shirin on the first days of the invasion and advanced on the Kermanshah and Ilam fronts (Sar-e Pol-e Zahab, Gilan-e Gharb, Musian/Dehloran); the central-front lines were pushed back in Dec 1981-Jan 1982 and Iraq announced its withdrawal on 20 June 1982. Town-by-town dates are not established here.

cites.note: cross-check; Iraqi entry to Dehloran/Qasr-e Shirin 12 July 1988

controller_note: Bakhtiari constitutionalist khans (Samsam al-Saltaneh, Sardar As'ad)
note: Bakhtiari forces took Isfahan in early 1909 and, with Sardar As'ad (who entered the city on 14 May 1909 per Iranica), marched on Tehran with the Gilan force, which fell on 13 July 1909. Dates are approximate.

controller_note: Kalhor chiefs (Davud Khan, killed 1912 fighting for Salar al-Dowleh; his successor Abbas Khan), with Guran and Sanjabi subordinate
note: Iranica: Davud Khan Kalhor, who 'ruled the tribe in the early 1900s', started as a peddler and made himself 'the absolute master of the entire territory between Kermanshah and the Ottoman border', also subjugating the Guran and Sanjabi; he held the Qajar title Sardar-e Mozaffar and governed the Kalhor district. He was killed fighting for Salar al-Dowleh (1911 per British records and Wikipedia; 1912 per Iranica) and his successor Abbas Khan was imprisoned by Reza Shah in 1926. Before c.1900 the Kalhor were one of several tribes inside the province of Kermanshah, governed from the city by Qajar princes (Kalhor and Zangana levies served those governors, e.g. against the Bakhtiari in 1830), with no autonomous Kalhor ruler; those years are left as direct. The exact start of Davud Khan's ascendancy (c.1900) is approximate.

cites.note: cross-check; Qajar-era role of the Kalhor and Zangana under the governors of Kermanshah

controller_note: Salar al-Dowleh (Abolfath Mirza) with Kalhor, Jaf, Sanjabi and Lur followers vs. Bakhtiari/government forces
note: Mohammad Ali Shah's brother occupied Sanandaj by 17 July 1911, seized Kermanshah (given up to plunder) and, per Wikipedia, Hamadan; he marched on Tehran, won a first battle near Malayer and was decisively beaten near Saveh by Amir Mofakham Bakhtiari (his Kalhor ally Davud Khan died in this campaign: 1911 per the British records and Wikipedia, 1912 per Iranica). The revolt did not end there: he remained in the Kermanshah-Kurdistan area until Farman Farma's 1912 expedition (Persian Gulf Administration Report 1911-14: 'In July Salar-ed-Dowleh fled from Kermanshah, on the arrival of Farman Farma... and left for Luristan and Kurdistan'), so the end is moved from Dec 1911 to July 1912. Control of each town in between is not established; status stays contested.

controller_note: Committee for the Defence of Iran's Independence / National (Provisional) Government of Kermanshah under Nezam al-Saltaneh Mafi, backed by German and Ottoman agents
note: Nationalists left Tehran for Qom (Nov 1915) and set up an anti-Allied government at Kermanshah; Ottoman and German forces occupied the city in 1915-16. The government fell back before the Russian entry on 26 Feb 1916.

controller_note: Imperial Russian Caucasian Cavalry Corps (Gen. Baratov)
note: Russian forces broke through at Sahneh (22 Feb), took Bisotun (24 Feb) and entered Kermanshah on 26 Feb 1916; the Ottoman XIII Corps (Ali Ihsan) retook it on 2 July 1916.

cites.note: cross-check; Russian entry to Kermanshah 26 Feb 1916
cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

controller_note: Ottoman Empire (XIII Corps, Ali Ihsan) and German officers, with the returned Persian nationalist government
note: The Ottomans held Kermanshah from 2 July 1916 until their retreat after the fall of Baghdad (11 March 1917); the exact evacuation date is not established. Wikipedia ('Battle of Khanaqin') says the Russians occupied Khanaqin after Ali Ihsan was recalled to Baghdad in Feb 1917, so the Ottoman hold on Kermanshah ended between Feb and mid-March 1917; the exact date remains unknown.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
cross-check; Ali Ihsan recalled Feb 1917, Russians occupy Khanaqin

controller_note: Imperial Russia (Baratov's remaining troops, disintegrating after the revolution)
note: After the Ottoman retreat Russian forces re-entered the Kermanshah area; most Russian troops left Persia between December 1917 and March 1918, a few under Baratov passing into British service. Dates low-confidence.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

controller_note: British (Dunsterforce lines of communication, then Norperforce)
note: The British held the Mesopotamia-Kermanshah-Hamadan-Qazvin-Anzali road line; Dunsterville reached Hamadan in Feb 1918. The garrisons were progressively reduced; Norperforce withdrew on 21 April 1921. Persian civil authority continued.

controller_note: Britain (East India Company/Bombay Marine; Residency moved from Bushehr to Kharg)
note: Occupied on 19 June 1838 in response to Mohammad Shah's siege of Herat; the Persians lifted the siege on 9 Sept 1838 but, "owing to the shifty character of their subsequent diplomacy", the island was not evacuated until March 1842.

controller_note: Britain (naval force; island garrisoned through the Anglo-Persian War)
note: Occupied 4 Dec 1856; Iranica: held until spring 1858 although the main forces left in 1857.

controller_note: Ka'b sheikhs of Fallahiyeh, then Khaz'al (decrees of 1903 granting Fallahiyeh, Hendijan, Deh Molla and Mashur as perpetual holdings)
note: The Ka'b heartland and the coastal lands behind Mohammerah were held by Arab sheikhs acknowledging the shah. Pre-1897 holdings and rulers are only loosely characterised here.

controller_note: Sheikh Khaz'al (administrator of northern Khuzestan from 1907)
note: Sardar Mokarram (later Nezam al-Saltaneh) placed Khaz'al in charge of northern Khuzestan in 1907; by 1911 the governorship "does not confer any great powers, most of the country being under the rule of the Shaikh" with only Dezful and Shushtar outside his control.

controller_note: Khans of Boir Ahmad (Garmsir/Sardsir), the Noi and other Kuhgiluya khans; Mamasani chief Emamqoli Khan
note: The tribal khans fell foul of the Qajars (Mohammad-Taher Khan blinded c.1800) but generally ruled their districts under nominal Qajar suzerainty with the Fars governor's backing at times. Tang-e Tamradi (Aug 1930) was a major tribal defeat of Reza Shah's army.

controller_note: Boir Ahmad / Kohgiluyeh / Mamasani khans vs. Reza Shah's army
note: After the Tamradi defeat (heavy losses - Iranica Boir Ahmadi: "said to have exceeded 1,000 casualties"; Fars iv gives about 400 killed; Aug 1930) the khans eventually surrendered and were executed in 1932; a military government then imposed order for the next decade.

controller_note: Boir Ahmad and Kohgiluyeh khans (tribal political system "rebounded with amazing vigor")
note: After Reza Shah's abdication central authority collapsed locally and tribal politics revived. In 1962-63 two khans resisted land reform, ambushed government forces at Tang-e Gochestan/Gachina Pass and were crushed in June 1963; thereafter the area was under tight security-force control.

controller_note: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic
note: Kurdish forces took the towns and garrisons of Paveh and Marivan region in March 1979; the army retook Paveh in the August 1979 offensive and mountain areas remained insurgent until 1983-84.

controller_note: Sayyed Abd al-Hosayn Lari (Najafi Lari), a pro-constitution mujtahid
note: In 1909 he proclaimed a revolt, issued his own postage stamps (in use March-May 1909) and, per Iranica, "ruled Larestan until the spring of 1915", when the governor-general of Fars sent Habib-Allah Khan Qavam al-Molk to pacify it. Lorimer-based accounts have him driven from Lar and returning in August 1909 and later deported to Shiraz; continuity of control is uncertain.

controller_note: Qawasim (Qasimi) sheikhs of Lengeh (Sheikh Qazib ibn Rashid last)
note: The Qasimi sheikh administered Lengeh for the Persian government from about 1789 as revenue collector under the governor of Bastak/Fars. In Feb 1887 Persia created the "Gulf Ports" governorate; in September 1887 the Qasimi governorship was dissolved, Sheikh Qazib was arrested and a Persian garrison landed; Sheikh Mohammad ibn Khalifa briefly seized Lengeh in 1898-99 before Ahmad Khan Daryabeigi retook it in March 1899.

controller_note: Pish-e Kuh Lur tribes under their own chiefs (Qajar governor-general sat at Khorramabad)
note: The wali dynasty of Luristan was overthrown in 1796 and replaced at Khorramabad by a governor-general, but the highland tribes kept their own organisation; the Pish-e Kuh was "largely outside control" until Reza Khan's army went in (April 1921 onward).

controller_note: Lur tribes vs. Reza Khan's army
note: The army deployed to Luristan in April 1921, took Borujerd (Oct 1923) and Khorramabad (Nov 1923), met a major revolt in May 1924 and the last major engagement in 1926. Wikipedia says direct control came in 1928; Iranica says war dragged on to 1933 but migration was banned from 1929.

controller_note: Mukri khans/emirs of Mukriyan as Qajar-appointed hereditary governors (Sauj Bulaq/Mahabad)
note: Mukriyan, south of Lake Urmia, was ruled by hereditary Mokri khans who served the Qajars as governors of Savojbolagh (Sayf al-Din Khan, d. 1891/2, held the post several times; his son Hosein Khan was killed in the Ottoman attack of 1914). Their power was eroded after Ubeydullah's 1880 invasion: the Qajar state built the Savujbulagh garrison in 1883 (Sayadi 2019: 'a manifestation of the exclusion of the Mukris from the Qajar political power structure'), so 1883 is used as the end. Not independently dated to the month; some accounts keep Mokri influence into the 1910s.

cites.note: cross-check; Sayf al-Din Khan and Hosein Khan as governors of Savojbolagh

controller_note: Local Kurdish chiefs and the Society for the Revival of Kurdistan (Komala-i Jiyanewey Kurdistan, 1942) under Qazi Muhammad; Soviet zone
note: After the Iranian army collapsed in Aug-Sept 1941 Kurdish leaders returned and rearmed; Soviet forces held the zone to the north and the Iranian gendarmerie and army were driven out of the Mahabad area. Qazi Muhammad led the Komala (1942) and the KDP (founded Sept 1945). Per British-zone accounts, southern Kurdistan up to Sanandaj was under British occupation, while the Kurdish-held belt from Mahabad to Saqqez lay between the two zones; by 1945 the Iranian government effectively controlled Kurdish areas only south of the Saqqez-Baneh-Sardasht line. Start date approximate.

controller_note: Republic of Mahabad (Qazi Muhammad, president)
note: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') has Qazi Muhammad inaugurating the Kurdish Republic at Mahabad on 15 December 1945; Wikipedia gives 22 Jan 1946 for the formal proclamation and presidency. Because the question here is when a rival administration actually replaced Tehran's, 15 Dec 1945 is used (the formal proclamation of Jan 1946 is listed as its own event). Territory: Mahabad, Bukan, Naghadeh, Piranshahr and Oshnavieh (Sardasht usually added); the republic claimed but did not hold Urmia, Khoy and Salmas. After the Soviets left (May 1946) it was isolated; Iranian troops entered Mahabad on 15-17 Dec 1946.

controller_note: KDPI and allied Kurdish councils at Mahabad
note: Mahabad stayed in Kurdish hands from early March 1979 (KDPI held the military base) until the army, using F-4s and over 100 tanks, took it on 3 Sept 1979; Sardasht, Bukan and Piranshahr fell on 4-6 Sept. Start is approximate (Feb-Mar 1979).

controller_note: KDPI peshmerga vs. IRGC and army
note: Qasemlu returned to Mahabad on 20 Oct 1979 as rebels retook the town; in Nov 1979 Kurds held most roads and rural areas. After the spring 1980 government offensive retook the cities, the KDPI controlled "a major portion of Iranian Kurdistan, excluding the towns" in 1981-82; IRGC and Iranian forces drove them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI left for Iraq by early 1984.

controller_note: Nader Mirza Afshar (grandson of Nader Shah), backed by the Afghan rulers of Herat
note: After Agha Mohammad Khan's death (1797) Nader Mirza returned to Mashhad and styled himself sovereign of Khorasan. Fath-Ali Shah failed in 1799 and 1801, besieged the city in 1802 and Mohammad-Vali Mirza took it in early 1803; Nader was blinded and executed in Tehran. Reach beyond the Mashhad district is not established.

controller_note: Mohammad-Hasan Khan Salar (son of Asaf al-Dowleh) with local khans and ulama
note: Mashhad rose on 25 Aug 1848, just before Mohammad Shah's death in early September, and held out against Hamza Mirza and then Sultan Morad Mirza; besieged from June 1849, it surrendered on 13 or 23 March 1850. Salar was executed on 29 April 1850. Iranica dates the whole revolt c.1847-51; the day-level chronology comes from Wikipedia only.

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

controller_note: Ka'b / Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir) under Qajar suzerainty with Ottoman claims
note: The Ka'b and later Muhaysin sheikhs "were for two centuries the most powerful chieftains of south-western Persia". Muhammara's allegiance shifted between Persia and the Ottomans.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

controller_note: Ottoman Baghdad (Ali Rida Pasha) vs. Persia over the Muhaysin sheikhdom
note: In 1837 Ali Rida Pasha captured and destroyed Muhammara and the Ka'b paid homage to the Ottomans; the town was "alternately claimed and occupied" until the Second Treaty of Erzurum (31 May 1847), Article II, ceded Mohammerah and Khizr island to Persia. Duration of the Ottoman occupation is not established.

cites.note: cross-check; alternately claimed and occupied by Persia and Turkey until the 1847 Treaty of Erzurum

controller_note: Muhaysin sheikhs of Mohammerah (Hajji Jabir, Sheikh Thamer, Sheikh Yusuf)
note: After Erzurum the sheikhs remained semi-autonomous under Persian suzerainty.

controller_note: Britain (Indian Army expeditionary force, Gen. Outram)
note: Mohammerah fell on 26-27 March 1857 after naval bombardment; the flotilla reached Ahvaz on 1 April; hostilities ceased about 4 April and the Treaty of Paris was ratified on 2 May. British forces left in mid-1857 (the main force sailed for India in May-June because of the Mutiny); exact evacuation date not established.

controller_note: Muhaysin sheikhs; Sheikh Khaz'al Khan (sheikh from June 1897)
note: Khaz'al succeeded his assassinated brother Mazal in June 1897, was recognised as Sardar Arfa' (1902), enjoyed British protection (assurances 1899-1908; KCIE 1910/1917) and ruled a "semi-independent realm". On 6 Dec 1924 he submitted to Reza Khan at Ahvaz; he was seized on 18 April 1925 and held in Tehran until his death (27 May 1936). The 1857-97 part of this span is only loosely characterised.

controller_note: Sultanate of Muscat and Oman (Al Bu Sa'id) under lease from the Qajar shahs
note: Under a Persian firman of 1793/94 the Sultan administered Bandar Abbas, the Minab-Khamir coastal strip and the islands of Qeshm and Hormuz for 75 years (garrison of 120 Nubians and 80 Arabs in 1811). Mulla Hosein of Qeshm seized Bandar Abbas after 1804; the Qasimi and the Bombay Marine contested Qeshm c.1806-10. A 1855 accord limited the lease to 20 years at 16,000 tomans a year; the Qajars regained the port in October 1868 amid dynastic trouble in Muscat.

controller_note: Ottoman Empire (troops on the orders of the vali of Baghdad, with Sunni Kurdish tribes)
note: The Ottomans began occupying Persian frontier districts on 23 May 1906 (Behik in Baradost), taking Dasht, Mergever and parts of Sardasht, Bana, Ganjachin and Baradost; Mergever was occupied again on 3 Aug 1907. Pressure by Russia and Britain pushed them back around 1911-12; the withdrawal was incomplete and intermittent. End date is approximate.

controller_note: Col. Mohammad-Taqi Khan Pesyan, commander of the Khorasan Gendarmerie, at Mashhad
note: Pesyan was made military governor-general by the post-coup government on 2-3 April 1921. After Qavam al-Saltaneh became premier (late May) and sent Najd al-Saltaneh as governor, Pesyan resumed full control in July and defied Tehran until killed fighting Kurdish forces under Sardar Mo'azzaz Bojnurdi at Quchan on 3 Oct 1921. Wikipedia counts the 'Autonomous Government of Khorasan' from 2 April; the rebel phase is dated here from c. June-July.

controller_note: Valis of Pusht-e Kuh (hereditary Faili Lur 'Vali dynasty': Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara to c.1900-01, then his son Gholam-Reza Khan, titled Sarim al-Saltaneh/Sardar Ashrafi)
note: After 1796 the wali family withdrew from Khorramabad to Pusht-e Kuh, where 'quasi-autonomous governors (wali)' ruled until about 1929 (Iranica). Wali names confirmed: Hoseynqoli Khan Abu Qaddara, succeeded around 1900-01 by his son Gholam-Reza Khan, who 'only tacitly acknowledged his vassal status to the Qajars with annual tribute' (hence indirect), held the rank of major-general and fled to Baghdad with his valuables in 1928-29 rather than accept Reza Shah's invitation to Tehran; he died in Baghdad in 1939. An account of the vali fleeing to Iraq with Simko in 1922 is contradicted by this chronology.

cites.note: cross-check; citing Afshar Sistani 1993 and Amanolahi 2002

controller_note: Khozeimeh 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan Heshmat al-Molk; Amir Esma'il Shawkat al-Molk, to 1904; Amir Mohammad Ebrahim Shawkat al-Molk, governor 1904-1924, then his two nephews, incl. Amir Ma'soum Khan, 'the last ruling amir')
note: Hereditary local rulers of Birjand/Qa'en acknowledged the Qajars and acted as their governors (Iranica: 'in practice the administration of large parts of [Khorasan] was in the hands of local tribal khans', among them the Khozeima 'Alam of Birjand and the Qa'enat). Shawkat al-Molk was governor 1904-1924; he resigned in 1924 handing power to two nephews and moved to Tehran, was governor of Fars 1937 and returned to Birjand in 1942 (d. 1944). The family's hereditary hold ended sometime in the 1930s; no source gives a date, so 1935 is a marker only. Mirza Rafi' Khan's rebellion from the citadel of Furg (1850s) was put down.

controller_note: Qashqai ilkhanis (Jani Khan, ilkhani from 1818/19; Mohammad-Ali Khan 1823-52; Mohammad-Qoli Khan 1852-67/8; Esmail Khan Soulat al-Dowleh from 1904)
note: The Qashqai ilkhanate controlled Fars' grazing lands and routes, bowing to the shah at times (Mohammad-Ali Khan was held at court in 1836) and dominating Fars during the weak central rule of 1909-21 (1911 civil war with the Qavami; anti-British rising in 1918; Soulat al-Dowleh reinstated as ilkhani by Mosaddeq in late 1920). This phase ends in 1926: Iranica says that in 1926 Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were summoned to Tehran as deputies and became virtual prisoners, and 'military governors were assigned to the various Qashqai tribes' with conscription and a new tax system - i.e. direct rule 1926-29. Highly variable autonomy; treated as a single phase.

controller_note: Qashqai (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan) and allied tribes vs. Reza Shah
note: The 1929 rising began in spring (the Khamseh Baharlu drove officials out of Darab at the end of April and took Fasa on 9 May); on 4 June the Qashqai closed the Bushehr road and then the Isfahan road, isolating Shiraz, which was under siege by mid-June; on 10 July the government flew Soulat al-Dowleh from prison to Shiraz to negotiate; the Khamseh occupied the eastern towns and the Baharlu reached the Kerman frontier; by summer the rebels held 'the whole province of Fars' outside the cities (Iranica 'Fars iv'). It ended with the August 1929 truce and amnesty. The truce withdrew the military governors; the abortive 1932 rebellion is not documented as holding territory.

cites.note: cross-check; summarising the British Persian Gulf Administration Reports 1926-38: Darab end April, Fasa 9 May, roads closed 4 June, Soulat released 10 July

controller_note: Qashqai under Nasser Khan (ilkhani) and Khosrow Khan, with German agent Schulze-Holthus from 1942
note: After Reza Shah's abdication (16 Sept 1941) the brothers escaped from Tehran, proclaimed themselves ilkhani and resumed nomadism; Persian troops were dispatched only in spring 1943 and heavy fighting followed (200+ soldiers killed at Semirom, 1943).

controller_note: Qashqai (Nasser Khan) under a treaty granting autonomy and arms in exchange for army garrisons
note: The 1943-44 agreement left the tribes armed and largely self-governing while allowing garrisons; the confederacy enjoyed "almost complete autonomy" through 1945-53.

controller_note: Southern tribes' "Sa'adun"/South Resistance movement vs. the Qavam government
note: In September 1946 Nasser Khan convened a conference of the southern tribes which rose against Qavam; the Qashqai took Kazerun and Abadeh and broke through Shiraz's outer defences until Qavam dismissed the Tudeh ministers and met demands (Oct 1946). Duration about one to one and a half months.

controller_note: Qashqai (Four Brothers: Nasser, Malek-Mansur, Mohammad-Hosein, Khosrow Khan)
note: Near-complete autonomy continued until the 1953 coup; in 1954 the brothers were exiled and their property confiscated.

controller_note: Qashqai insurgents (Khosrow Khan Qashqai) vs. IRGC
note: After an attempt to arrest Khosrow Khan in June 1980, Qashqai insurgents "defied the central government" for two years from camps in the mountains until a night attack by the Revolutionary Guards in April 1982; Khosrow Khan was executed on 8 Oct 1982. This was a mobile insurgency from mountain camps, not control of the Qashqai counties; the Revolutionary Guards held the towns and roads. Shown at low confidence: control may in fact have stayed direct.

controller_note: British North Persia Force (Norperforce)
note: Formed 16 Sept 1918 from Dunsterforce remnants with its HQ at Qazvin, the main body at Manjil and a battalion at Zanjan; about 6,000 men in 1918, 3,600 by 26 Oct 1920; completely withdrawn into Mesopotamia on 21 April 1921, leaving its arms to the Persian Cossacks. Persian administration continued.

controller_note: Za'faranlu Kurdish ilkhanis of Quchan (e.g. Reza-Qoli Khan, defeated by Abbas Mirza in 1832; Sam Khan)
note: Kurdish khans held the Quchan marches as hereditary governors, fielding thousands of horsemen and acknowledging the shah only intermittently. Reza Khan's bombing of Bojnurd (18 May 1925) opened the end of the Kurdish ilkhani system; end date is therefore a convenience marker, not a precise date for Quchan. Abbas Mirza razed the Quchan fortress and exiled Reza-Qoli Khan after the 1832 battle (13,000 Kurds against 19,000 men); Iranica nonetheless says the Za'faranlu kept their tribal structure and ilkhani leadership throughout the Qajar era (Sam Khan fought for the shah against Salar and at Herat), and that Chenaran and Darreh Gaz were 'from time to time' under the governor of Khorasan's direct rule. So 'indirect' is retained, with brief direct episodes.

controller_note: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
note: Tabriz was taken on 13 Oct 1827, Urmia on 28 Jan 1828 and Ardabil on 8 Feb 1828. Turkmenchay (22 Feb 1828) tied evacuation to indemnity instalments. Kinneir reported on 12 March 1828 that he had negotiated 'the immediate evacuation of Azerbijan, with the exception of Khoee' and that the Russians were 'duly preparing to withdraw'; Paskevich left Tabriz in March. The end is therefore set at April 1828 (low); Khoy is mapped separately.

cites.note: cross-check; Tabriz 13 Oct 1827, Urmia 28 Jan 1828, Ardabil 8 Feb 1828
Paskevich leaving Tabriz, evacuation of Khoy tied to indemnity instalments

controller_note: Hasan Khan Salar and his Turkmen/Kurdish/local allies
note: After Hamza Mirza withdrew, Salar dominated most of Khorasan; the government counter-offensive retook Sabzevar (9 March 1849) and Neyshabur (21 March 1849). Start date is approximate (late summer/autumn 1848).

cites.note: cross-check; the only source consulted giving the 1848-50 day-level chronology

controller_note: Ardalan valis of Senneh (Sanandaj); last wali Amanollah Khan Ardalan
note: The Ardalan family ruled Kurdistan as hereditary vali under the Qajars. In 1284/1867-68 Naser al-Din Shah ended the vilayet's special status and appointed his uncle Farhad Mirza Mo'tamed al-Dowleh governor of the province of Kurdistan.

controller_note: Kurdish groups (KDPI, Komala, local councils) vs. the Islamic Republic (army, IRGC)
note: Kurdish groups seized garrisons in Sanandaj (17-19 March 1979), Saqqez, Marivan and Paveh; Khomeini declared jihad on 17 Aug 1979 and the government retook Sanandaj and Saqqez by early September. In 1981-82 the Kurds held most of the countryside outside the towns; IRGC pushed them out in 1982-83 and the KDPI withdrew to Iraq by early 1984 (Komala persisted slightly longer). Towns and countryside flipped repeatedly; the whole span is coded contested.

controller_note: Shahsevan tribal khans ("the time of the independent khans")
note: Russia closed the Moghan frontier to the Shahsevan in 1884 and between 1884 and 1922 the Shahsevan operated with minimal central authority. They were among the first major tribes pacified and disarmed by Reza Khan's army in winter-spring 1922-23. Status before 1884 (Qajar-appointed governors with tribal chiefs) is not recorded here. Iranica ('Shahsevan'): 'virtually independent of central government for nearly four decades'; the chiefs 'usually controlled the region... focused on the city of Ardabil and smaller urban centers' until Reza Khan's army pacified them in winter-spring 1922-23; a Russian force of 5,000 under Gen. Fidarov campaigned against them in 1912. They are shown as outside state control because Iranica describes no acknowledgment of the shah; autonomy under the shah is arguable.

controller_note: Ismail Agha "Simko" of the Shikak (base at Chehriq castle)
note: Simko established authority west of Lake Urmia in 1918-19, plundered Urmia in winter 1920, defeated government forces at Tasuj (March 1921) and was joined in summer 1921 by the Mamash, Mangur and Piran. He was defeated by Reza Khan's army in summer 1922 and fled to Iraq; he returned and rebelled again in 1926 and was killed on 30 June 1930 at Ushnu. Persian authority existed only in a few towns.

controller_note: Simko and the Shikak
note: Wikipedia (single source) places Mahabad (Sauj Bulaq) in Simko's hands after the death of Maj. Malakzadeh and about 600 gendarmes in October 1921, with control extending to Sardasht and Baneh by 1922. Treat as low-confidence.

controller_note: Local Sistani chiefs (Sarbandi, Kayani maliks; Ali Khan Sarbandi) with Persian and Afghan claims overlapping
note: Sistan was disputed between Persia and Afghan rulers and run by local chiefs. Ali Khan accepted Persian allegiance in 1857, unpopularly. The Goldsmid arbitration of 1872 awarded Persian (west) Sistan to Persia; Persian governors followed from December 1873.

controller_note: Persian governors with the 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat (Mir 'Alam Khan, then Shawkat al-Molk)
note: Iranica: Mir 'Alam Khan drove insurgents out of Sistan and added it to his Qa'enat amirate under Naser al-Din Shah. Sistanis rebelled against the Qa'en chief in Dec 1872 (shut him in Nasirabad); a Persian governor (Samsam al-Mulk, then Mohammad Ja'far Khan, Dec 1873) followed.

controller_note: British India: East Persia Cordon (July 1915), Seistan Force (from March 1916; commander Col. J. M. Wilkeley, then R. E. H. Dyer from Feb 1916)
note: British-Indian troops held Sistan to bar German agents from Afghanistan; the Persian governor remained but the force dominated Nasratabad and the border. The cordon later extended north via Birjand to Mashhad and (from 1918) to the Transcaspian line. Last elements left Persia in November 1920.

cites.note: cross-check; formation July 1915, Seistan Force from March 1916, last elements out Nov 1920

controller_note: 'Alam amirs of Qa'enat as governors of Sistan
note: After the British withdrawal the Alam family governed Sistan and Qa'enat as quasi-hereditary governors: Shawkat al-Molk had full authority in 1921 and resigned in 1924 in favour of two nephews (Iranica). Weakly documented; the 1935 end is a marker only.

controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
note: Sykes landed at Bandar Abbas in March 1916 to raise the South Persia Rifles (authorised strength 11,000; about 3,300 infantry and 450 cavalry by mid-1917); the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Persian civil governors remained. Whether this deserves the occupation label is debatable (the Qajar government assented under pressure). Kerman (from June 1916) and Shiraz (from Nov 1916) are mapped separately.

controller_note: Hereditary governors of Tabas (Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas' family; Zangu'i khans; Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' under Naser al-Din Shah)
note: Per the Gazetteer of Persia vol. I (c.1910) the Tabas governorship was hereditary: Nader Shah gave the district to 'Ali Murad Khan of the Zangu'i (Arab, related to the Khozeima amirs of Qa'en) and 'the same family still govern[s] the district'; the older Vakil-i-Tabas family also held it. Haji Mohammad Baqer Khan 'Emad al-Molk' (d. 1894) was succeeded by his eldest son 'Ali Akbar Khan. The khan paid a fixed sum to the shah and was otherwise left to do much as he pleased. The family was still in office around 1910, so the end cannot be earlier; no source gives its end, so 1935 is an estimate tied to Pahlavi centralisation.

cites.note: Tabas governorship hereditary in the family of Mir Hasan Khan 'Vakil-i-Tabas'; also Iranica 'Khorasan xi' extract naming the Zangu'i khans of Tabas

controller_note: Anjoman of Tabriz and constitutionalist fighters (Sattar Khan, Baqer Khan)
note: Tabriz refused Mohammad Ali Shah's coup of 23 June 1908 and withstood a royalist siege for ten months until Russian troops entered on 30 April 1909. The city sought to restore the constitution, not to secede.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

controller_note: Imperial Russia (General Snarski's expeditionary force; later Russian garrisons in Tabriz and along the Julfa road)
note: Russian troops held Tabriz from 30 April 1909; after the Fedayeen attack of 21 Dec 1911 Russia re-entered after shelling on 31 Dec 1911 and executed about 1,200. Russia evacuated on 17 Dec 1914 and the Ottomans (Kurdish irregulars and regulars) held Tabriz 8-31 Jan 1915 (under a month) before Russia returned; last Russians left 28 Feb 1918. Iranian administration continued throughout.

cites.note: cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

controller_note: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
note: Ottoman forces entered Tabriz on 8 June 1918 (Wikipedia's other date: 18 June) and left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918); exact evacuation date not established.

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations
cross-check; 30 Apr 1909 - 28 Feb 1918, break 17 Dec 1914 - 31 Jan 1915

controller_note: Khans of Tangestan, Dashtestan and Dashti (Zair Khidr, Shaikh Hosein Khan of Chah Kutah) under the governor of Bushehr
note: Tribal khans of the Bushehr hinterland controlled their districts and acknowledged the Qajars loosely. Baseline characterisation only.

controller_note: Tangestani/Dashti tribal forces (Rais Ali Delvari, killed 2 Sept 1915; Shaikh Hosein Khan Chahkutahi; Zair Khidr) with German agent Wassmuss vs. the British and pro-British khans
note: The tribes attacked the British Residency at Bushehr on 12 July 1915, fought the British after the occupation of Bushehr (8 Aug 1915) and kept the hinterland in revolt, joined by the Qashqai in 1918, until the rising subsided (influenza, British pressure). Some sources say Tangestani resistance lasted to 1921.

controller_note: Qara'i khans: Eshaq Khan (strangled 8 July 1816) then his son Mohammad Khan (1816-32)
note: Eshaq Khan Qara'i ruled Torbat-e Heydarieh as a quasi-independent magnate under Fath-Ali Shah (at times effective master of Mohammad-Vali Mirza's Khorasan). Abbas Mirza captured Mohammad Khan by trickery in 1832, ending Qara'i independence; afterwards Qajar-appointed governors ruled.

controller_note: Yomut and Goklen (Guklan) tribal leaders
note: Turkmen of the Gorgan plain raided Khorasan and Astarabad and beat Persian armies (1858 near Qarri-qal'a; 1860 at Merv). Qajar governors of Astarabad held the town and a few forts; the plain itself was outside effective Persian control. Some Goklen paid taxes or migrated under pressure.

controller_note: Turkmen tribal chiefs under nominal Persian governors of Astarabad (Persian posts, tax-collection, Russian border pressure)
note: After the Russian conquest of the Akhal Teke and the Akhal-Khorasan convention (1881) the Yomut/Goklen lost their steppe hinterland and were drawn into limited Persian tax/administrative arrangements. Reza Khan's army moved in and disarmed the Turkmen in 1925; Gonbad-e Qabus became the settlement centre. The 1881 start is a convenience marker.

controller_note: Turkmen People's Councils / Turkmen Cultural and Political Society vs. IRGC
note: After the Revolution Turkmen councils (shuras) ran local affairs; open clashes in March 1979 ended in a ceasefire on 3 April, with renewed fighting in May and August 1979 and in February 1980; by early 1980 the IRGC had occupied the Turkmen towns. The councils did not secede, and control of towns flipped; included for completeness at low confidence.

controller_note: Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri and his Kurdish tribal host (Ottoman and Iranian Kurds) vs. Qajar forces from Tabriz
note: Tens of thousands of Kurds crossed into north-west Persia in autumn 1880, took Sauj Bulaq (Mahabad) and Maragheh, failed to take Urmia (its Shia population refused to surrender) and withdrew after about eight weeks. Exact start/end dates not fixed in the sources consulted. Wikipedia ('Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah') says Ubeydullah's son Abdulqadir 'retreated to Mahabad, which they held for a few days' before Qajar forces from Tabriz arrived, and that after about eight weeks the rebels retreated; Urmia held out. Control was transient and set up no administration, so it is shown as contested (low confidence).

cites.note: cross-check; ~8 weeks, Mahabad and Maragheh taken, Urmia held out
cross-check; Mahabad held a few days; withdrawal after eight weeks

controller_note: Assyrian/Armenian forces, Simko's Shikak and local Persian notables after Russia's withdrawal
note: Russian troops left Azerbaijan between Jan and March 1918. Simko murdered the Assyrian patriarch Mar Shimun on 3 March 1918; Assyrians, Armenians and Kurds fought for the Urmia plain until the Ottomans arrived. Control was fragmented and short-lived.

controller_note: Ottoman Empire (IV Corps)
note: Dilman (Salmas) fell on 18 June and Urmia on 31 July 1918; Ottoman forces left after the Armistice of Mudros (30 Oct 1918).

cites.note: cross-check; Ottoman and Russian dated operations

controller_note: United Kingdom (Persia and Iraq Force), later joined by the US Persian Gulf Command (from Dec 1942) in Khuzestan
note: British forces entered Khuzestan, took Abadan and the Ahvaz oilfields and advanced from Iraq via Kermanshah to Hamadan in Aug-Sept 1941. Iranian administration continued. The Allies withdrew from Tehran on 17 Oct 1941; British (and US) troops left by 2 March 1946 under the Tripartite Treaty.

controller_note: Soviet Union (44th and 47th Armies)
note: Soviet troops took Tabriz and Ardabil by 26 Aug 1941. Iranian civil administration continued; the Tripartite Treaty (29 Jan 1942) declared the presence not an occupation and required withdrawal within six months of the end of hostilities (2 March 1946).

controller_note: Azerbaijan People's Government (Democratic Party of Azerbaijan; Ja'far Pishevari, premier) under Soviet protection
note: The Democrats took Tabriz around 20-21 Nov 1945 and proclaimed the Autonomous Government of Azerbaijan on 12 Dec 1945 while Soviet troops blocked the Iranian army. Soviet forces left in May 1946; Iranian forces began moving in on 9 Dec 1946 and entered Tabriz on 12-13 Dec 1946, when Pishevari fled to Baku. Dating: Iranica ('Azarbaijan v') says all major routes into the province were seized by the Democrats by 19 Nov 1945, an Iranian column of 1,500 troops was stopped at Qazvin by the Soviets, and Tabriz was 'in the hands of the Democratic Party' by 10 Dec 1945; Wikipedia has 21 Nov. The Soviet-held zone therefore reached the Qazvin line. Zanjan province is included on the strength of general accounts; Iranica does not name it (the Iranian advance of Dec 1946 is said to have moved on Zanjan, but no source was found here).

controller_note: Soviet Union (based at Mashhad and Bojnurd)
note: Soviet troops entered Khorasan on 3 Shahrivar 1320 (25 Aug 1941) from Sarakhs, Dargaz and Bajgiran and occupied the north-east, based at Mashhad and Bojnurd; Iranian civil administration continued. Iranica ('Khorasan xi') says the Soviets stayed 'until the winter of 1943', but the Soviet communique of 25 Feb 1946 announced that evacuation of 'Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan' would begin on 2 March 1946, and on 24-25 March the Soviets (via Kennan, FRUS) said it 'has already been finished' (Mossadegh doubted this on 3-4 March). 'Winter of 1943' is probably a mis-conversion of winter 1324 Sh. (1945-46). The end date is the Soviet claim of completion; the south-east (Birjand, Tabas) was not in the Soviet zone.

cites.note: Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished

controller_note: Soviet Union
note: Soviet forces took Gilan (Anzali, Rasht), Mazandaran and Gorgan in August 1941 and reached Qazvin; they entered Tehran on 17 Sept 1941 and withdrew from it by 17 Oct. Iranian civil administration continued. The last Soviet troops left on about 6-9 May 1946. Semnan province, evacuated by 24 March 1946, is mapped separately.

controller_note: Baluch chiefs of Sarhad (Rigi, Ismailzai, Damani, Baranzai) who had come to terms with the Persian governor of Bampur; Persian officials at Bampur, Khash and Nasratabad
note: Gazetteer of Persia vol. IV (c.1908-10): the power of the Sarhad chiefs 'continued almost undiminished', although 'within the last few years' they had submitted to the Persian governor of Bampur, and a small Persian party from Bampur, Khash or Nasratabad could pass through Sarhad levying taxes or blackmail on chiefs and headmen. That is acknowledgment of the shah's governor by local chiefs (indirect), not a total absence of state authority. Koyagi: Qajar presence 'waned significantly' after 1906, leaving a vacuum that raiding exploited. The 1850-1900 stretch is weakly documented (Persian garrison at Bampur from 1850) and may have been 'none'; the status shown is a low-confidence compromise. Frontier demarcated 1895-96.

controller_note: Soviet Union
note: Soviet forces held Semnan province (Shahrud, Damghan, Semnan) on the Tehran-Mashhad route from the August 1941 invasion; Iranian civil administration continued. Evacuation of Shahrud and Semnan began on 2 March 1946 and was reported finished by 24-25 March (FRUS 1946 VII, doc. 282). Split from the other Soviet-held provinces, which were evacuated until about 6-9 May 1946.

cites.note: Soviet statement that evacuation of Meshed, Shahrud and Semnan, begun 2 Mar 1946, was finished

controller_note: Imperial Russian army (Gen. Paskevich)
note: Khoy was held as a deposit until the whole indemnity was paid. Kinneir's letters show the Russians still in Khoy on 14 and 25 Aug 1828 (he suspected they hoped to occupy it indefinitely), and his dispatch of 26 Nov 1828 reports the withdrawal from Khoy in exchange for a large Persian payment (with a 100,000-toman gift from Paskevich on receipt). End set to Nov 1828 (low); the start month is not established (after the fall of Tabriz on 13 Oct 1827).

controller_note: Qashqai ilkhani family (Soulat al-Dowleh, Nasser Khan, Khosrow Khan), reinstated in the Majles after the truce
note: After the 1929 truce Soulat al-Dowleh and Nasser Khan were reinstated as deputies, the military governors were withdrawn from tribal territory and a general amnesty was declared (Iranica). The Qashqai rebelled again in 1932 'but in vain', Soulat al-Dowleh died in prison in 1933 and the army then cut the migration routes; direct control followed. Low confidence on both ends.

controller_note: Pro-German officers of the Fars Gendarmerie and Democrat Party members (with the Tangestani khans and the German agent Wassmuss as allies)
note: On 10 Nov 1915 the Gendarmerie seized the government buildings of Shiraz and arrested the British consul (Maj. O'Connor) and the British colony, having 'openly declared with the Germans and revolted against their own Government' (India Office file); Iranica places the expulsion of the British-backed acting governor Habib-Allah Qavam al-Molk in late 1915. His son Ebrahim Khan Qavam al-Molk, with a British-aided tribal army and pro-British gendarmes, took the city back in April 1916 and became acting governor-general. Gendarmes also seized Kerman and Yazd in the same crisis according to Wikipedia, but without dates; not mapped. Rebel-held for about five months.

controller_note: Babis led by Mulla Mohammad-'Ali Hojjat al-Eslam Zanjani (about 2,000 fighters and their families) vs. the governor and the shah's army
note: The Zanjan 'upheaval' began on 13 May 1850; from about 19 May the town was divided in two, with the Babis holding their fortified quarters against the governor and then against the army that gathered from June (Aziz Khan Mokri, commander-in-chief, arrived on 25 Aug). Hojjat died on 29 Dec and the last Babi positions fell in a general assault about 2 Jan 1851. An eight-month armed enclave, shown as contested because the town was split rather than ceded to a separate government. The Babi stand at Shaykh Tabarsi (Mazandaran, late 1848-May 1849) and the Neyriz rising (1850) were also armed enclaves but were not mapped (single fort / weeks).

cites.note: 13 May 1850 - 2 Jan 1851; low-grade source, cross-check only

controller_note: Imperial Russia (Cossack and line garrisons at Urmia, Khoy and Salmas)
note: Wikipedia ('Persian campaign (World War I)') says Russia occupied Tabriz in 1909 and Urmia and Khoy in 1910 to secure the road from Julfa to Van; Russian consulates and garrisons controlled the Urmia plain until the Russian withdrawal of Jan-Mar 1918. In Dec 1914 the Russians pulled back to one brigade around Salmas and Urmia and the Ottomans held Urmia from 4 Jan 1915 and briefly Salmas/Dilman; the Russians returned from early Feb 1915 (the Tabriz record treats the same break as under two months). Persian civil administration continued. Start month and extent are approximate (Salmas on the strength of the 1915 fighting at Dilman).

cites.note: cross-check; Russian occupation of Urmia and Khoy in 1910; Dec 1914 withdrawal; Jan-Mar 1915

controller_note: British Indian Army (Indian Expeditionary Force D, 6th Poona Division) guarding the Anglo-Persian Oil Company refinery
note: On 6 Nov 1914, the day after Britain's war with the Ottoman Empire began, Indian Expeditionary Force D occupied Fao and then Abadan island, where Sheikh Khaz'al (who rented the island to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909 and administered it until 1924) allowed the British to garrison the refinery; a small force went up the Karun to Ahvaz in Feb-Mar 1915 (Battle of Ahvaz, 3 Mar 1915). The withdrawal date is unknown; the Armistice of November 1918 is used. Treated as foreign occupation despite the sheikh's consent, like the Bushehr and SPR records.

cites.note: cross-check; IEF D occupies Fao and Abadan, 6 Nov 1914

controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
note: Sykes's column reached Kerman on 12 June 1916 and an SPR brigade was stationed there by December 1916; Persian civil governors remained and the force was disbanded in 1921 after the coup. Same caveat as the Bandar Abbas record (assented under pressure).

controller_note: British-officered South Persia Rifles (Sir Percy Sykes) with Indian Army support
note: Sykes marched into Shiraz on 11 Nov 1916 with the new governor-general Farman Farma (Iranica 'Fars iv'); an SPR brigade stayed there until the force was disbanded in 1921. Persian civil governors remained; same caveat as the other SPR records.
